The selected words describe the apple that Gregor's father threw, which has stayed lodged in Gregor's back as an unremoved reminder of his injury.

Its meaning is that nobody in the family is willing to take the apple out, so it stays in his flesh, and it shows how serious his wound is. It also suggests that his family, despite their revulsion at him, still treats him as a relative who cannot simply be discarded, as the next sentences in the document make clear p. 47.

text:
The passage is Grete's line that the family must get rid of Gregor, spoken during their exhausted family conversation on page 62.

The line appears in the family's late-evening discussion after the three lodgers have given notice. Grete, speaking now only to her father, says they cannot go on living this way, that Gregor's presence will be the death of both parents, and that she can no longer endure it. The phrase "get rid of it" refers to Gregor, whom she has already begun calling "this monster" and "it", not "my brother". It marks the moment the family turns from pity and patience toward a plan to remove him. The reader should note the line is spoken by Grete, not narrated, and that it is followed on page 63 by her insistence that "that's not Gregor" and that he must be dismissed.

The passage is narrative, so I give the strongest alternative reading. The sister's line that the family must "get rid of it" can be read as the story's moral verdict: family duty has been exhausted and Gregor's humanity is abandoned. A critic could object that the text does not license this, since the sister's words are an emotional outburst from a character who has been exhausted and whose judgment is shaped by resentment, and the narrator keeps Gregor's inner sense of love and sympathy in view. Reading her line as a plain endorsement risks flattening that tension.

The sister's rhetoric is tied to her fatigue, her tears, and her sense that "it's got to go", and it comes immediately after Gregor has been driven back by violence. Her language also shifts from "it" to "this monster" to "that's not Gregor", showing the family's self-justification at work rather than neutral judgment.

Kafka's text does not state an author's reply in this passage, so the strongest response available is that the narrative presents the family's logic through the sister's voice without endorsing it.

text:
Gregor's father threw it. At the end of Part II, he comes home in his bank uniform, finds that Gregor has got out of his room, and assumes Gregor has done something violent, as he says "Just as I expected" p. 44. He fills his pockets with fruit from the sideboard and bombards Gregor, one apple after another, without careful aim p. 46. Most glance off, but one lodges in Gregor's back p. 46.

It matters for a few reasons. The wound is permanent: no one dares remove the apple, so it stays "as a visible reminder" and costs Gregor much of his mobility p. 47. It also shifts the family's attitude. The injury reminds even the father that Gregor is still a family member, to be treated with patience rather than as an enemy p. 47. And it keeps hurting and festering until the end, when Gregor can barely feel "the decayed apple in his back" as he dies p. 65.

Reading it as a symbol of the father's violence or of the family's guilt goes beyond what the text states.

text:
The document gives Grete's own reasons in her speech, and a few causes can be read from the surrounding pages, though the text never states her motives as a single explanation.

What she says is that the family is worn out. They have "done all that's humanly possible" to look after Gregor, and she claims it "'ll be the death of both of you." She says they cannot work so hard and then come home "to be tortured like this" p. 62. She also blames him for driving out the tenants and claims he wants to take over the flat p. 63. Her argument that "that's not Gregor" lets her justify abandoning him: a real Gregor would have left of his own free will p. 63.

The trigger is the scene with the lodgers. Gregor's appearance in the living room ruins her violin playing and costs the family their rent, and the middle gentleman gives notice p. 61.

Earlier pages show the buildup. She has to work at a sales job, and she has become indifferent in her care of him, pushing food into his room with her foot p. 51. The narrator also notes her early difficulty bearing his appearance p. 35.

Why her feelings shift so completely is left to interpretation; the narration gives no direct statement of her inner state.

Part III

Part III follows the Samsa household in the weeks after Gregor's injury, as the family's patience and money wear thin. It brings the story to its close, so it settles what Gregor's transformation finally means for the people around him.

Where we are

Gregor lies injured in his room, an apple lodged in his back, more than a month after his father's attack. p. 47
The family is poor and exhausted: the maid is gone, jewellery is sold, and everyone works, though the flat is too big for their means. p. 50
A room in the flat has been let to three bearded gentlemen, and clutter and rubbish are being pushed into Gregor's room. p. 54

People

Gregor — The transformed son, once the family's provider, now weak, mostly confined to his room, and watching them through the door.
Grete — His sister, who works in a shop, studies shorthand and French, and plays the violin; she once cared for Gregor closely.
Mr. Samsa — The father, now working as a bank employee, who wears his uniform even at home and dozes in his chair.
Mrs. Samsa — The mother, asthmatic, who sews underwear for a fashion shop and wants to look after Gregor.
The charwoman — A strong elderly widow who does the heavy work and is not afraid of Gregor.
The three gentlemen — Fussy, tidy lodgers who take a room in the flat and expect order.

Threads to watch

The family's patience with Gregor is stretched by money worries and fatigue, and the care for him is changing. p. 51
Grete's claim over cleaning Gregor's room causes a bitter family row and shows how her feelings toward him have shifted. p. 52
Gregor, still drawn to music and to his old plan for Grete, wonders whether he is an animal at all. p. 58
The lodgers' presence puts pressure on the household to keep Gregor hidden. p. 55
